we aim to extend GOIO to more complex scenarios, such as multi-class imbalanced classification and long-tailed distributions.
In our experiments, we employed 18 real-world tabular datasets and five artificial datasets to evaluate the performance of our model.
All the real-world datasets used in our experiments are publicly available, sourced from repositories including UCI [48] and the Python package imbalanced-learn [49].
We generated five synthetic datasets based on two multivariate Gaussian distributions following [50], enabling precise control over dataset characteristics for clearer result interpretation.

TABLE II DESCRIPTION OF ARTIFICIAL DATASETS

Essential details for these real-world datasets, including the selected target class (# T) as of minority class for binary classification, data size (# S), feature length (# F), and the class imbalance ratio (IR), are summarized in Table I.
Class overlap in the synthetic datasets is controlled by varying the mean of the positive class while keeping the negative class mean fixed at 0.
Each dataset consists of 4,000 samples from two classes
IR = Nmaj / Nmin, (16) where Nmaj and Nmin represent the number of majority and minority class instances, respectively.

For each dataset, we apply stratified 5-fold cross-validation, randomly splitting the data into five folds. In each iteration, one fold is used as the test set, while the remaining four folds are used for training.
Each experiment is repeated with ten random seeds to ensure reliable results, and the average performance across all runs is reported.
Resampling methods are applied to balance the class distribution within the training set, after which classification models are trained on the transformed data and evaluated on the test set.
In each table, we report the mean and standard deviation of each metric, followed by the rank of each method in parentheses, with the best rank highlighted in bold.
